title: The Chaldeans
hook: Iraq's Catholics still pray in a form of Aramaic; Francis visited them in 2021

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Thomas Christians of India, who name an apostle as the one who brought them the faith. Your line was thomas's children. Did a doubt of yours find words? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.

"Talitha cumi." Jesus takes a dead girl by the hand and says those words, and she gets up. Mark's Gospel sets them down as they sounded, and only then stops to translate: damsel, arise. He could have given the meaning alone. Instead he leaves the words standing, like stones in a field, so a reader hears the sound of the voice. Readers take them as Aramaic, the speech of Jesus's world. Now go to northern Iraq, to a village church on the plain near Mosul, or a church in Baghdad. On Sunday, the priest and people pray in Syriac, a form of Aramaic. Words from the same family as talitha cumi, still in the mouths of a living congregation. Today is the church that kept them.
screen: `TALITHA CUMI.` → `ARAMAIC LEFT STANDING IN MARK.` → `STILL PRAYED IN IRAQ.`

segments.voice: The name reaches back to Abraham. Genesis says his family set out from Ur of the Chaldeans. The Chaldean Catholic Church takes its name from that old region, in what is now Iraq. Its people speak of themselves as heirs of some of the earliest Christian communities of Mesopotamia. Then the language. Mark keeps Aramaic more than once. On the cross, he writes, Jesus cried, "Eloi, Eloi, lamma sabacthani?" and then translates it: my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Syriac, the language of the Chaldean liturgy, is a form of Aramaic, written in its own script. When Chaldeans pray the Our Father in Syriac, the sound is a near neighbor of the sound in that Galilean house. Next, the hard years. Iraq's Christians have lived through war, and in recent years families fled when an extremist group overran their towns on the Nineveh Plain. Churches were burned. Some families came back to rebuild; others now pray in Syriac far from home. And then a visit. Pope Francis traveled to Iraq, prayed among the ruins of Mosul's churches, and went to Ur, the place of Abraham, to pray with Muslims, Yazidis and others who honor Abraham too. A pope standing where Abraham's journey began, beside a church that still prays in that language family. Last, look back at this week. A Divine Liturgy sung almost entirely. A wall of icons. A baby given everything at once. A priest's wife with a title. Cedars in Lebanon. Thomas's children in India. And now Chaldeans in Iraq. One Catholic Church, many ancient homes.
screen: `UR OF THE CHALDEANS.` · `ARAMAIC: STILL PRAYED, IN SYRIAC.` · `RUINS, FLIGHT, AND A RETURN.` · `A POPE AT UR.` · then, large: `TALITHA CUMI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Iraq, or keep it company. Settle, and breathe. Picture a church with smoke stains on its walls, and a family sweeping the floor anyway. Picture the rivers, the markets, the neighbors of every faith who've also lost homes. Let all of them in. If you pray, you can pray for Iraq and everyone who lives there, or just say the Our Father slowly, knowing it's being prayed in Syriac somewhere today. If you don't pray, sit with the people sweeping that floor, and wish them a whole roof. The bell holds the time.
The Chaldeans. Iraq's Eastern Catholic church, named for the land of Abraham, praying in Syriac, a form of Aramaic. The last stop of this week. Today's word.

Your line: the language of jesus. Today, say talitha cumi once under your breath, get up from whatever is keeping you down, and remember who still speaks that language family. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Chaldean Catholics celebrate the Holy Qurbana in the East Syriac tradition, praying in Syriac and Arabic and, abroad, in local languages; their patriarch is based in Baghdad, and Chaldean parishes abroad serve families who left Iraq.

original.note: Aramaic words written in Greek letters in Mark 5:41, which the Douay-Rheims translates: damsel, arise.

trapdoor: what you thought: nobody speaks Jesus's language anymore.
what it means: Iraq's Chaldean Catholics still pray in Syriac, a form of Aramaic, the language family of talitha cumi.

what a scholar hears: Syriac is a literary Aramaic dialect with its own script; Jesus's Galilean Aramaic was a different dialect of the same language, so Syriac is a close relative rather than the same speech.

sources.ref: Pope Francis's apostolic journey to Iraq

notes: Index hook dates Pope Francis's visit to 2021 (March 5–8, 2021); the script omits the year under the claims rule. Confirm: prayer in Mosul's Hosh al-Bieaa square among ruined churches, and the interreligious meeting at Ur with Muslims, Yazidis, Sabeans/Mandaeans and others.

The flight from the Nineveh Plain and Mosul when the so-called Islamic State overran them (2014) is mentioned without a date or number and without naming the group; 'many families fled' is a softened claim. Confirm the wording is careful and fair to Iraq's Muslim neighbors, who are also named among those who lost homes.
Genesis 11:31 paraphrased as 'Ur of the Chaldeans' (Douay-Rheims and KJV wording differ: 'Ur of the Chaldeans' / 'Ur of the Chaldees'). Confirm.
Mark 15:34 translation paraphrased in voice ('my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me') following the Douay-Rheims gloss; confirm exact wording, and the Douay-Rheims spelling 'lamma sabacthani'.
Chaldean self-description as heirs of early Mesopotamian Christianity: attributed to them, no date. Confirm.
Week look-back (days 1359–1365) is in the teach: Divine Liturgy, iconostasis, infant initiation, married priests, Maronites, Thomas Christians, Chaldeans.
Original: ταλιθα κουμ (Mark 5:41); manuscripts vary between κουμ and κουμι. Confirm.

Editor: hook rewritten so it no longer asserts as fact what Mark 'could have written in Greek' or that these are 'the language Jesus actually spoke'; it now leans on Mark's own translation ('damsel, arise') and says readers take the words as Aramaic.
